faqs.a: It is a guaranteed return equal to your rate (6.5% = 6.5% risk-free). It makes sense if your rate is high or you value being debt-free; investing may win mathematically at low rates. Keep an emergency fund first either way.
faqs.q: Is it smart to pay off my mortgage early?

faqs.a: With most mortgages, extra principal shortens the term - your required payment stays the same but you finish years earlier. Recasting (a separate lender process) is what lowers the payment.
faqs.q: Do extra payments shorten the loan or lower the payment?

faqs.a: Start early - dollars added in year 2 kill far more interest than dollars added in year 20. Automate a fixed extra amount monthly rather than relying on willpower.
faqs.q: What is the best extra-payment strategy?

faqs.a: Most do automatically, but some apply it to future payments. Specify principal only in writing or online, and verify on your next statement.
faqs.q: Will my lender apply extra to principal?

faqs.a: A lump sum today beats the same total spread monthly, because it starts killing interest immediately. But monthly extra is easier to sustain - the best strategy is the one you will keep.
faqs.q: What about a lump sum vs monthly extra?

mortgage-payoff-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = APR / 12 / 100
Lump sum reduces the balance first, then each month: interest = balance x r; principal = payment - interest.
Months is about -ln(1 - balance x r / payment) / ln(1 + r). Simulated month-by-month here.

keyFacts: Extra mortgage payments go straight to principal, skipping you ahead in the amortization schedule.

mortgage-payoff-calculator.quickAnswer: On a $280,000 mortgage at 6.5% with a $1,770 payment, adding $300 extra a month cuts payoff from 30 years to about 20.4 - saving roughly 9.6 years and $130,000 in interest. Enter your loan to find your mortgage-free date.

mortgage-payoff-calculator.workedExample:
$280,000 balance, 6.5% APR, $1,770/month, +$300 extra:
1. Monthly rate = 0.541667%. Base payment $1,770, accelerated $2,070.
2. Without extra: about 360 months (30 years), about $357,200 total interest.
3. With $300 extra: about 245 months (20.4 years), about $227,150 total interest.
4. You save about 115 months (9.6 years) and about $130,000 in interest.
